research.premium_liability: The employer owes the premium. Under 268B.14 subd. 1, premiums "accrue and become payable by each employer," and each employer pays them to the state every quarter. The commissioner assesses the premium against the employer's premium account (268B.13). Under Minn. R. 3317.5000 subp. 5, the employer "remains liable to the commissioner for premiums." If the employer fails to pay, the employee keeps the right to benefits (268B.14 subd. 9). Employees have no direct liability to the state. Their part is a "charge back": the employer may deduct it from wages (268B.14 subd. 3).

research.can_employer_elect_to_pay_employee_share: Yes. Minn. Stat. 268B.14 subd. 3 sets only a floor on the employer's part: "a minimum of 50 percent." Employees pay "the remaining portion, if any, of the premium not paid by the employer," so an employer that pays 100% leaves the employee nothing to pay. For small employers, subd. 5a(b) works the same way, with an employer minimum of 25% of the full rate. DEED says this explicitly in a presentation it gave the Senate Jobs committee on 2025-04-02 (archived by the Legislative Reference Library): "Employers may choose to pay more than their required portion for some or all employees." Its October 2025 union-worker deck says the same ("Employers can cover more than 0.44% if they chose"). DEED's September 2025 employer deck tells employers to "Decide how to split premiums." Under 268B.26(b)(2), each employer must tell its employees the amount of premium deductions it makes, which confirms that the amount differs from employer to employer.

rate_2026.total_rate: 0.88% of taxable wages (medical 0.61% + family 0.27%). DEED's commissioner set this under 268B.14 subd. 7 ('may adjust the annual premium rates ... prior to January 1, 2026'); it replaces the statutory 0.7% in subd. 6. Small employers (30 or fewer employees and an average wage at or below 150% of the statewide average) pay 75% of that rate, 0.66%, under subd. 5a.
rate_2026.max_employee_share: 0.44% of taxable wages: the 0.88% total minus the employer's minimum 50% (subd. 3). For small employers it is also 0.44%: the 0.66% total minus the employer's minimum of 25% x 0.88% = 0.22% (subd. 5a(b)). DEED confirms 'small employers can deduct up to 0.44%'. The minimum employee share is 0%, because the employer may pay everything. Under an approved private plan, employees cannot be charged more than they would pay under the state plan (268B.10 subd. 2(5)).
rate_2026.wage_base_or_cap: About $185,000 for 2026. 268B.01 subd. 43 sets taxable wages up to the Social Security OASDI maximum rounded to the nearest $1,000. SSA's 2026 base is $184,500 (Federal Register, 2025-11-03), and DEED's December 2025 document states the cap as $185,000. 268B.14 subd. 4 states the cap without the rounding, so it would read $184,500. The cap does not bind for any benchmark household under about $184,500.

research.summary: Minnesota Paid Leave premiums are owed by the employer (Minn. Stat. 268B.14 subd. 1: premiums 'accrue and become payable by each employer'; Minn. R. 3317.5000 subp. 5). The employee part is a statutory 'employee charge back' (subd. 3). The employer must pay at least 50% of the premium (at least 25% of the full rate for small employers under subd. 5a), and employees pay through wage deductions only 'the remaining portion, if any, of the premium not paid by the employer.' The employer may choose to pay more, up to the whole premium, so the employee share runs from 0% to 0.44% of wages. DEED's guidance says the same: employers 'can deduct up to 0.44%' and 'may choose to pay more than their required portion'. Each employer must tell employees how much it deducts (268B.26(b)(2)), and private plans cannot charge employees more than the state plan would (268B.10). For 2026 the total rate is 0.88%, set by the DEED commissioner under subd. 7 and announced around 2025-02-21; small employers pay 0.66%. The maximum employee share is 0.44% for both sizes, on wages up to the Social Security base rounded to the nearest $1,000 (about $185,000). All of this was published well before 2026-07-03, and the revisor shows no 2026 change to ch. 268B. The engine applies 0.44% unconditionally, and documents that it assumes 'the employer withholds the maximum permitted employee share.' For scenario_032, 0.0044 x $29,000 = $127.60, which equals the legal maximum exactly; I confirmed the figure by running the engine. That amount is an upper bound, not a mandatory one; the legal floor is $0. Classification: optional employer pass-through.

verdicts.reasoning:
Statute lens. I fetched the full 268B.14 section, the full ch. 268B text, 268B.01, 268B.10, Minn. R. ch. 3317, Laws 2024 c 127, and 177.27. I also searched the whole chapter for deduct, withhold, charge, contribut, 'employee shall/must' and liability language.

1. Liability for the premium is entirely the employer's. Under 268B.14 subd. 1(a), premiums are 'payable by each employer', and each employer pays them quarterly. Under 268B.13, the commissioner assesses each employer's premium account. Under subd. 9, an employer's nonpayment does not affect the employee's rights. Under 268B.15 subd. 7(d), an employer that receives a refund must return any 'erroneously deducted' amounts to employees. Minn. R. 3317.5000 subp. 5 says the employer 'remains liable to the commissioner for premiums'. Nothing in ch. 268B makes the employee liable to the state, and the state has no collection path against employees for premiums.

2. The only employee-share text is the 'Employee charge back' in subd. 3 and the parallel subd. 5a(b)(2). Both use 'must' language: employees 'must pay the remaining portion, if any, of the premium not paid by the employer', and the employer 'must make wage deductions as necessary'. This is the strongest argument for refutation. But the size of the remainder is set by the employer's own election above a floor: 'a minimum of 50 percent' (25% of the full rate for small employers). 'If any' expressly contemplates a zero remainder. So the 'must' only stops an employer from deducting more than the remainder, or from taking the employer's own portion out of pay (subd. 5a(b)(1): 'Employers shall not deduct ... to fund the employer portion'). It does not require any positive employee amount.

3. The surrounding provisions support this reading:
- 268B.26(b)(2) requires employers to tell employees 'the amount of premium deductions made by the employer', so the amount varies by employer.
- 268B.10 subd. 2(5) and 3(5) only cap what private-plan employees can be charged.
- 177.27 subd. 4 lets DLI order compliance with 268B.14 subd. 3. That is wage-deduction protection for employees, not a withholding mandate.

4. DEED's own primary materials consistently describe the share as optional:
- 'Employers can deduct up to 0.44%' (December 2025).
- 'Employers may deduct the employee portion' (govdelivery bulletin).
- 'Employers may choose to pay more than their required portion for some or all employees' (Senate deck, April 2025, and the September 2025 employer deck).
- 'Employers can cover more than 0.44% if they chose' (union deck, October 2025).
- 'Action 1: Decide how to split premiums.'
- The employer deck also treats any amount above the minimum as an 'employer pickup' that is deductible as a business expense.

One DEED line says the reduced small-employer premium 'does not change the amount owed by employees'. In context that refers to the 0.44% maximum, not a mandatory amount.

This fits category (b) exactly: the premium is the employer's liability, and the employer may, but need not, deduct up to 0.44% of taxable wages. Calling it mixed or unclear would overweight the conditional 'must', which binds only after the employer has chosen its own share.

verdicts.reasoning:
Through the administration lens the sources support the classification.

1) Liability. The statute places the premium on the employer. 268B.14 subd. 1 says premiums "accrue and become payable by each employer." Under 268B.13 the commissioner assesses each employer's premium account. Interest, liens and levies under 268B.15 and 268B.23 run against the employer. Minn. R. 3317.5000 subp. 5 says the employer "remains liable to the commissioner for premiums." Nothing in ch. 268B or Minn. R. ch. 3317 makes an employee liable to the state for premiums that were not deducted. An applicant owes the state only for benefit overpayments under 268B.185. Subd. 9 keeps the employee's rights intact if the employer fails to pay. 268B.15 subd. 7(d) requires the employer to refund wrongly deducted amounts to employees, which treats the deduction as the employer's charge-back mechanism.

2) May or must. The administrative rules (Minn. R. ch. 3317, published 2025-07-09 at 49 SR 1368) say nothing about how the premium is split. The only related text is a private-plan notice item describing "the process to calculate and collect employee contributions." Every DEED source I read uses permissive language. The bulletin says "Employers may deduct the employee portion." The 2025-12-19 PDF says "Employers can deduct up to 0.44%." The roles page says "you can deduct a maximum of .44%." The FAQ says "can collect up to 0.44 percent... may choose to pay more." The calculator page says employers "can optionally choose to cover a higher percentage." The September 2025 employer deck tells employers to "Decide how to split premiums."

3) Can the employer choose to pay it? Yes. Subd. 3 fixes only an employer floor of 50%, or 25% of the full rate for small employers under subd. 5a. The employee pays "the remaining portion, if any, of the premium not paid by the employer." The "must" in subd. 3 and in subd. 5a(b)(2) ("must make wage deductions as necessary") applies only to whatever the employer has chosen not to pay. It does not set a fixed employee amount. The employer must notify each employee of "the amount of premium deductions made by the employer" (268B.26(b)(2)), which assumes the amount varies by employer. This matches the benchmark's option (b): the premium is the employer's liability, and the employer may, but need not, deduct up to a share.

4) Rate, share and cap. The total is 0.88%, split 0.61% medical and 0.27% family, set under the subd. 7 adjustment authority. Small employers pay 0.66%. The maximum employee share is 0.44% for both sizes, which I recomputed from the statute and confirmed in DEED documents. The cap is the OASDI base of $184,500 (Federal Register, 2025-11-03), rounded to $185,000 under 268B.01 subd. 43. The statutory split rule took effect 2026-01-01 (Laws 2024 c 127 art 73 s 38) and appears in the 2025 Statutes, whose PDF was created 2025-10-19. The revisor's Table 2 lists no 2026 Regular Session actions for ch. 268B, though it does list 2026 actions for ch. 268. All of this was published before 2026-07-03.

5) Engine. I read the source and ran it. It applies a flat 0.0044 rate to wages capped at $185,000, and its documentation says it assumes "the employer withholds the maximum permitted employee share." The aggregator's documentation calls its components "mandatory" employee payroll taxes, but for Minnesota the component is the legal maximum, not a mandatory amount. For scenario_032 the engine's $127.60 equals the legal maximum exactly. The legally possible range is $0 to $127.60. The deduction also cannot push pay below the applicable minimum wage; that limit binds only if the hourly wage is within about 0.44% of the minimum wage, and the prompt gives no hours.

Nuance that does not change the result. DEED's taxes page (modified 2026-05-08) says an employer that pays more than its minimum share is giving the employee additional compensation, taxable as wages. It also says the employee may deduct the full amount "that the employer pays on their behalf (up to .44% of wages)" as a state income tax. So for federal tax purposes, an employer pickup is still treated as the employee's 0.44%, paid through extra wages. That is how the federal government characterizes a choice the employer makes. It does not create any state-law duty to deduct, so the share remains an optional employer pass-through.

All key quotes were confirmed. The one gap in the rate's provenance is that I could not read the bot-blocked press release, and the dated DEED PDFs cover that gap. Not refuted.

I read all of Part 5 of Article 13.3 (8-13.3-501 through 524) myself in the OLLS CRS 2025 Title 8 PDF, plus the definitions in 503. Then I searched the whole part for 'deduct', 'withh', 'shall pay', 'employee shall', 'liab' and 'contribut'. In covered private employment, the only premium-payment duty falls on the employer: 507(2) says the employer 'shall remit' premiums 'for each employee'. Section 507(5) is the only provision on employee deductions, and it is permissive in both sentences: 'may deduct up to 50 percent'. The employer still 'shall remit' 100% (10 or more employees) or 50% (fewer than 10).

The 'shall pay' language appears only in 507(4)(a)-(b). It applies to self-employed people and employees of opted-out local governments who elect coverage under 514, and they remit directly. 507(9)(b) confirms that local-government employees owe nothing unless they elect coverage. 509(2)'s 'shall continue to pay' concerns health-benefit cost-sharing during leave, not premiums.

- 502(4)(a), a findings clause, authorizes the enterprise to 'collect insurance premiums from employers and employees'.
- 511 requires the program notice to describe 'payroll deduction requirements'. The rules give that content: an employer must not deduct more than the employee share, and a missed deduction cannot be clawed back.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute the classification through the administration lens and could not. Every primary source I read supports 'optional employer pass-through'.

Statute: I downloaded the OLLS CRS 2025 Title 8 PDF myself (Last-Modified 2025-09-16). In C.R.S. 8-13.3-507(2), the duty to remit falls on the employer alone ('an employer shall remit'). 507(5) gives employers of both sizes the power that they 'may deduct up to 50 percent' of the premium from wages, while they 'shall remit' 100% (10 or more employees) or 50% (fewer than 10). Part 5 imposes a payment duty on an individual only in 507(4): self-employed people and local-government employees who opt in under 8-13.3-514. 507(9)(b) confirms that an opted-out local government's employee 'is not required to pay' unless they elect coverage. The findings clause 502(4)(a) mentions collecting 'from employers and employees', but it is not operative. 507(7) says premiums are 'fees and not taxes'.

Rules: I read both the current 7 CCR 1107-1 (effective 01/01/2026; adopted 10/31/2025; Colorado Register 12/10/2025, per the SOS history page I fetched) and the original 2022 version. In both, an employer that fails to deduct the maximum 'is considered to have elected to pay that portion of the employee share'. The current rule bars the employer from recovering it later except when wages were insufficient, and fines over-deduction. Neither version contains any provision that makes the employee liable when no deduction is taken. The only 'owes' provision (1.4(3)) applies to individuals electing coverage.

Agency guidance: I fetched famli.colorado.gov with curl and a browser user agent, because WebFetch got a 403. The agency says employers 'may deduct up to 50%', that 'Some employers may choose not to deduct', and it refers to 'employers that are choosing to deduct'. The 2026 headcount notice says all employers have the 'Option to deduct up to 0.44%'. Some looser FAQ wording ('collect and remit the 0.44% of the employee's share'; 'should be deducting') is informal guidance that conflicts with the agency's own 'may choose not to deduct'. It cannot override the statute's 'may' or the rule's deemed election.

So the employee's legal liability is $0, and up to 0.44% of capped wages is at the employer's discretion.

Rates and dates: SB 25-144 session law ch. 293 (approved May 30, 2025; the bill page says effective 08/06/2025) sets 0.88% for 2026. The OASDI base of $184,500 is in 90 FR 49047, published 2025-11-03. All of these predate 2026-07-03. I found one 2026-session FAMLI bill, SB26-127; it was postponed indefinitely on 2026-04-09 and does not touch premiums.

Engine: I read the engine source this session. co_employee_famli_contribution = employee_rate (0.0044 from 2026-01-01) x min(max(0, employment_income), SS cap of 184,500). It does not depend on employer headcount or on any employer-deduction choice, and it carries no documented 'employer deducts the maximum' assumption. The Minnesota variable does carry that assumption ('withholds the maximum permitted employee share'). employee_state_payroll_tax's documentation calls its components 'mandatory', which does not hold for Colorado. research.premium_liability: The employer owes the contribution. Under M.G.L. c. 175M s. 6(a), the employer (or covered business entity) "shall remit" the contributions for each employee to the Family and Employment Security Trust Fund. Under s. 7(d), employers, covered business entities and electing self-employed individuals "make contributions". 458 CMR 2.05(5) defines the employer's portion as whatever it does not deduct from wages, and says the employer "in all instances" pays and remits the remainder. 458 CMR 2.05(7) penalizes the employer for failing to remit and bars it from recouping from employees an allowable deduction it failed to take. The employee owes nothing to the state directly. Their only exposure is a wage deduction the employer chooses to take, up to the statutory caps. The exception is self-employed people who elect coverage: they are responsible for all contributions (s. 6(b)).

STATUTE LENS. I downloaded and read all eleven sections of M.G.L. c.175M from malegislature.gov. I searched every section for deduct, withh, 'employee shall', 'employees shall', payroll and contribut. No section says an employer 'shall deduct' or 'shall withhold', and none makes the employee liable to the fund. The only operative text on the employee portion is a set of ceilings. Section 6(c)(1) says an employer 'shall not deduct more than 40 per cent' of the medical contribution, and 6(c)(2) says it 'may deduct not more than 100 per cent' of the family contribution. Both add that the employer 'shall remit the full contribution'. Every liability provision names the employer side. Section 6(a) says the employer or covered business entity 'shall remit'. Section 7(d) lists who 'make contributions' as employers, covered business entities and self-employed individuals, and employees are left out. Section 8(g) assesses the employer that 'fails or refuses to make contributions', treats contributions as taxes under c.62C, and treats them as debts. Section 6(d) relieves small employers of the 'employer portion' but says they 'shall remit' 100% of family and 40% of medical. It does not require them to deduct those amounts. The only person the statute makes pay their own contributions is an electing self-employed individual (6(b)).

REGULATION. 458 CMR 2.05(5), which I read in a Wayback capture of the official mass.gov PDF (the live URL returns 403), says the employer 'may deduct up to certain defined percentages'. It defines the employer's portion as the part 'not deducted from wages'. It makes the employer 'in all instances' responsible for the remainder. Subsection (5)(c) expressly covers an employer that 'opts to deduct a lower percentage' and still requires it to remit the full amount. Subsection (5)(d) allows different percentages for different groups. Subsection (7) bars an employer that 'failed to properly assess the allowable deduction' from recouping assessments from employees. Cornell LII, a secondary source, shows 2.05 was last amended in 2020, and I found no later amendment requiring deductions.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE CONSIDERED. Four things point the other way. The s.1 definition of 'Contributions' includes payments by 'an employee'. Section 4(a)(ii) requires notice of 'the employee's contribution amount and obligations'. The DFML Overview, in every capture from November 2025 to September 2026, says 'employers must withhold PFML contributions from employees' paychecks'. And Acts 2026 c.101 s.43 refers to 'tax burdens on employees'. These show that the law contemplates an employee contribution when the employer chooses to deduct one. None of them imposes a minimum deduction. The DFML sentence is non-binding summary language, and the same paragraph says employers 'may choose to cover a larger share... for some or all of their employees'. The same page tells small employers they 'may elect to cover some or all of the covered individuals' share'. Statute and regulation control, and both are permissive with a ceiling and no floor. research.premium_liability: The covered employer carries the liability. Under WCL s.211, a covered employer "shall, with his or her own contributions and the contributions of his employees, provide" DBL and PFL benefits. It does so by insuring with the State Insurance Fund or a private carrier, by self-insuring, or through a Board-accepted plan. The premium is owed by the employer to its carrier; it is not a contribution paid to the state. Under WCL s.210(1), the employer pays the DBL cost "in excess of the contributions collected from his or her employees". So if the employer collects nothing, the employer bears the whole cost. Employees owe nothing directly to the state or the carrier. Any employee money reaches the premium only through employer payroll deductions, which WCL s.209(4) authorizes but does not require. When the employer deducts, it acts as the employees' agent (WCL s.209(5)). For PFL, the employer must return any surplus over the premium (12 NYCRR 380-7.2(b)(3)). Penalties for failing to provide coverage fall on the employer (12 NYCRR 380-7.2(d)).

caveats: Classification is the same for PFL and DBL: both are optional employer pass-throughs. The difference is in default design. PFL is designed to be paid entirely by employees: s.209(3)(b) bars requiring employers to fund it, and DFS sets the rate to cover the full premium. DBL is cost-shared: the employee pays at most 0.5% up to $0.60 a week and the employer pays the rest (s.210). For both, collection is at the employer's discretion: s.209(4) 'authorized', and WCB says 'allowed, but not required'.

Textual tension. WCL s.209(1) says every employee 'shall contribute ... to the extent and in the manner herein provided'. The DFS 2026 decision says 'Employers shall collect employee contributions consistent with this Decision'. The WCB press release calls PFL 'fully paid for by employees'. The operative mechanism, however, is permissive: s.209(4) 'is authorized to collect' and 12 NYCRR 380-7.2(b)(1) 'may deduct'. The WCB employer page explicitly says collection is 'allowed, but not required'. I read 'shall collect consistent with this Decision' as limiting how much may be collected, not as a mandate to collect.

Benchmark implication. The prompt defines payroll_tax to include 'mandatory employee state payroll taxes'. Under NY law, the DBL and PFL employee contributions are not mandatory withholdings. The engine's $443.11 is the maximum an employer may collect, so it is correct only if one assumes the employer deducts the maximum, and the prompt does not state that assumption. The NY engine files do not state it either. The cross-state aggregator documentation labels these contributions 'mandatory', which conflicts with the NY primary sources above.

Board-accepted plans and collective bargaining agreements (WCL s.211(4)-(5)): employer and employee obligations follow the plan or agreement. Employee contributions may exceed the statutory amounts only 'by agreement' and when reasonably related to the value of the benefits. Such a plan may also require less or nothing. s.209(4) defers to these plans.

Self-insured employers (s.211(3)) and employers insured through the State Insurance Fund or private carriers: the choice of funding method does not change the discretionary nature of employee deductions.

Public employers: WCL s.201(4) excludes the state, municipal corporations, local governmental agencies, other political subdivisions and public authorities from 'employer'. Public-sector workers therefore have no DBL or PFL deduction unless coverage is extended another way. The PFL site says requirements for other employer types differ; I did not fetch the public-employer opt-in provisions. The prompt does not say whether the employer is public or private.

Small employers: there is no small-employer exemption. Per s.202, which I read in summary plus a short quote, a private employer with one or more employees on each of at least 30 days in a calendar year is covered. Domestic or personal employers in a private home are covered only for workers who meet an hours threshold (about 20 hours a week, per the fetched summary).
Employee-level exemptions and waivers reduce or eliminate the deduction:
- DBL: an employee receiving or entitled to Social Security old-age benefits may be exempt by filing Form DB-130 (WCB employer page).
- PFL: may be waived by employees who are regularly scheduled under 20 hours a week and will not work 175 days in a year, or who work 20+ hours but won't be employed 26 consecutive weeks.

- s.201(5) excludes some categories of worker from 'employee', for example clergy, an executive officer who owns all of a corporation's stock, and certain professional or teaching roles at religious, charitable or educational institutions.
Multiple jobs (DBL): combined contributions across jobs may not exceed $0.60 a week, and the employee may ask the employers to prorate (WCB pages). The engine does not model this.

The DBL cap is weekly, not annual. The engine's annual min(0.5% x annual wages, $31.20) can differ from the law's maximum for workers with uneven weekly wages, for example some weeks under $120. It can also differ in years with 53 weekly paydays (law maximum $31.80). Neither difference matters for scenario_082.

Two further limits on PFL: the employee's contribution may not exceed the per capita share of the actual annual premium (s.209), and employers must refund any surplus over the premium (12 NYCRR 380-7.2(b)(3)).

Catch-up deductions: s.209(4) lets an employer that skipped a deduction collect it within one month after paying the wages. 12 NYCRR 380-7.2(c) bars recovering missed PFL withholding by later withholding above the weekly maximum.

The employee shares the engine counts for both NY DBL and NY PFL are optional employer pass-throughs, not mandatory withholdings.

**Who owes the cost.** The covered employer must provide the coverage by insuring with the State Insurance Fund or a private carrier, self-insuring, or using a Board-accepted plan (WCL s.211), and it owes the premium to its carrier.

**Employee share.** WCL s.209(4) "authorizes" the employer to collect the employee share by payroll deduction. Agency guidance says this directly: the WCB employer page says the employer "is allowed, but not required, to collect contributions" for both programs, and paidfamilyleave.ny.gov/cost says "An employer may choose to pay for the Paid Family Leave benefit on behalf of employees." For DBL, the employer pays whatever it does not collect (s.210). The 2026 caps an employer may collect are:
- **PFL:** 0.432% of wages per pay period, up to $411.91 a year (DFS decision dated Aug 29, 2025; equal to 0.432% x NYSAWW $1,833.63 x 52).
- **DBL:** 0.5% of wages, up to $0.60 a week (statutory since 1950).

**Engine check.** For scenario_082 ($100,195 wages) the engine gives PFL $411.91 and DBL $31.20, a total of $443.11. I re-ran it this session and got the same figures, which exactly equal the law's maximum employee shares. So the match holds only if the employer deducts the maximum, an assumption the NY engine files do not state. The engine's cross-state aggregator also calls these contributions "mandatory".

**Caveats that change who pays:**
- Collective-agreement or Board-accepted plans, where contributions may be higher by agreement, lower, or zero.
- Public employers, which are excluded from "employer".
- The DB-130 exemption for Social Security old-age beneficiaries, and PFL waivers for short-hours or short-tenure employees.
- Proration across multiple jobs for DBL.

verdicts.reasoning:
I read the statute and rules myself, and they support the classification for both programs: the employee share is an optional employer pass-through, not a mandatory withholding.

**Who owes the premium.** The employer does.
- WCL s.211 requires the covered employer to provide DBL and PFL benefits through the State Fund, a carrier, self-insurance or an accepted plan.
- s.213 makes a non-complying employer 'fully and directly liable' for the benefits.
- 12 NYCRR 380-7.2(b)(2) contemplates the employer paying the premium before it collects any employee contributions.
- s.210(1) and (3) put the DBL cost 'in excess of the contributions collected' on the employer.

**How the employee share reaches the premium.** Only through the employer's payroll deduction, which the law permits but does not require.
- s.209(4) says the employer 'is authorized to collect' by payroll deduction. If it skips a pay period, it may catch up only within one month after paying the wages.
- 12 NYCRR 380-7.2(c) bars recovering missed PFL withholding by later withholding above the weekly maximum. So contributions the employer does not collect are simply never owed.
- 11 NYCRR 363.3(i), the DFS regulation, defines the PFL maximum employee contribution as the most 'a covered employer is authorized to collect'. 363.7(b) defers collection to s.209.
- 12 NYCRR 380-2.5(d) refers to contributions 'required by the employer of like employees', which treats requiring them as the employer's choice.
- The agencies say it directly. The WCB employer page says collection is 'allowed, but not required' for both DB and PFL. The WCB employee page says the same for DB. paidfamilyleave.ny.gov/cost says 'An employer may choose to pay for the Paid Family Leave benefit on behalf of employees.' DFS calls the 2026 maximum what an employer is 'authorized to collect'.

**Where 'shall deduct' or 'shall withhold' language would appear, it does not.** I searched Article 9 for it. s.209 says 'authorized'. s.220 (penalties) has nothing on employee deductions. s.213 addresses only employer liability.

**Contrary text.** Some language frames the employee as obligated:
- s.209(1): every employee 'shall contribute ... to the extent and in the manner herein provided'.
- 12 NYCRR 380-2.6(b) and (d): employees 'shall make regular' PFL contributions, and become 'obligated' once the employer notifies them.
- The DFS decision: 'Employers shall collect employee contributions consistent with this Decision', and the employee is 'not liable' for more once the cap is reached.
- The WCB press release says employees 'will contribute' and calls PFL 'fully paid for by employees'.

These describe the employee side, and the default design: PFL is meant to be fully employee-funded (s.209(5); 'No employer shall be required to fund'). But 'the manner herein provided' is employer collection, which s.209(4) makes permissive. The official PFL site expressly allows the employer to absorb the cost. No primary source makes the employee liable to the state or the carrier independent of the employer collecting, and none requires the employer to withhold.

**DBL versus PFL.** For DBL the case is even clearer. The employee share is capped at $0.60 a week, the employer pays the balance by statute, and both the WCB fact sheet and Form DB-271S say employers 'may collect'.

**Engine.** The engine counts the maximum permitted share for both programs: PFL $411.91 + DBL $31.20 = $443.11 for scenario_082, which equals the legal maxima. The NY variables and parameters state no 'employer withholds the maximum' assumption; a grep for 'assum' and 'maximum permitted' found nothing. Meanwhile the employee_state_payroll_tax aggregator's documentation labels these 'mandatory', which NY primary law does not support.

**Verdict.** The quotes check out and the classification stands. The research overstates the reach of 380-7.2(b)(1) and omits the 380-2.6 and DFS 'liable' language, but neither changes the result.

- s.209(4) says the employer 'is authorized to collect' the employee contribution through payroll deductions, and only within one month after paying the wages.
- s.209(5) makes the employer the employees' agent when it collects.
- s.210(1) has the employer pay the DBL cost 'in excess of the contributions collected', so whatever is not collected falls on the employer.
- s.211 makes the covered employer the party that must provide the benefits.
- s.209(3)(b) bars requiring employers to fund PFL but does not bar them from doing so voluntarily.
- No subdivision says the employer 'shall deduct', 'shall withhold' or 'must collect'.

Regulations (12 NYCRR 380-7.2, via Cornell LII):
- (c) says missed PFL withholding cannot be recovered later by withholding above the weekly maximum.
- Together with the one-month window in s.209(4), nothing makes the employee liable for a contribution the employer did not deduct.
- Penalties for failing to provide coverage fall on the employer (380-7.2(d)).

Agency guidance:
- The WCB employer page says 'An employer is allowed, but not required, to collect contributions' and covers both DB and PFL.
- The WCB employee page says the same for DB.
- The WCB DB fact sheet and Form DB-271S both use 'may collect'.
- paidfamilyleave.ny.gov/cost says 'An employer may choose to pay for the Paid Family Leave benefit on behalf of employees.'
- DFS defines the 2026 maximum as the amount an employer is 'authorized to collect'.

Counter-evidence I weighed:
- WCL s.209(1): 'Every employee ... shall contribute ... to the extent and in the manner herein provided.' The manner provided is permissive employer collection under s.209(4).
- DFS: 'Employers shall collect employee contributions consistent with this Decision' and 'the employee shall not be liable for any additional contributions' after the cap. I read both as setting the ceiling and method of collection, not as a mandate to collect.
- The PFL employer-responsibilities page: 'Ensure that you are collecting the employee contributions that pay for this insurance.'
- The WCB press release: PFL is 'fully paid for by employees'.

These describe the default design, especially for PFL, which DFS rates so that the employee share covers the full premium. None of them requires deduction. I tried to refute the classification from the statute, reading the full chapter rather than only the quoted lines. I downloaded cga.ct.gov chapter 557 (2026 Supplement and current/pub) with curl. The first fetch used -k; a later plain curl returned HTTP 200. I read 31-49e (definitions), 31-49g, 31-49h, 31-49i through 31-49o, and 31-49q through 31-49u in full. I then searched every PFML section for 'may deduct', 'may withhold', 'deduct', 'withh', 'on behalf of' and 'employer may'.

Findings:
(1) 31-49g(b)(1) puts the obligation on the employee: 'each employee ... shall contribute'. 31-49h(b)(11)(E) repeats it ('each employee ... shall contribute').
(2) 31-49g(b)(3) requires withholding: every employer paying wages 'shall deduct and withhold' the contribution each payroll period.
(3) 31-49g(b)(4) lets the state collect from either the employee or the employer. Under (b)(6), an employer that does not comply faces penalties.
(4) The only 'may withhold' language in the PFML sections is 31-49o(c), for approved private plans. There, employees owe nothing to the state fund, and the employer's deduction of up to the state rate is optional.
(5) No clause anywhere in 31-49e to 31-49u lets an employer pay instead of withholding, or makes the share for public-program employees optional.
(6) The contribution applies to 'each employee', defined in 31-49e(7) as an individual serving an employer in Connecticut, not only to a 'covered employee'. So the $2,325 quarterly test affects benefit eligibility only, not who contributes.
(7) 'Employer' covers anyone with one or more employees. Only governmental and certain school employers are excluded, unless their employees bargain in.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute the classification through the administration lens and could not. The primary sources I read myself support it.

Statute: 31-49g(b)(1) puts the duty on the employee, who "shall contribute" a percentage of subject earnings up to the Social Security base. The rate is set by the Authority at no more than 0.5%. Under (b)(3), every employer paying wages "shall deduct and withhold" the contribution each payroll period. Under (b)(4), the state can collect from a non-paying employee or employer after notice. Under (b)(5)-(6), employers must register and report, and face penalties. The (b) text is identical in the Jan. 1, 2025 revision and the 2026 Supplement.

Formal rules: the only Connecticut regulations in this area (31-49p) cover appeals. Contribution rules sit in the Authority's Consolidated Policies, adopted under CGS 1-121.

Agency wording is uniformly "must"/"required", never "may":
- "you are required to withhold payroll deductions of 0.5%" (for-businesses page)
- "required to withhold 0.5% of employee wages" (employer fact sheet, Oct. 2024)
- individuals "may not opt-out" (contributions page)
- the program is "entirely employee funded" with "no employer match" (for-businesses page)

Can an employer choose to pay the employee share? No primary source authorizes that. Withholding is mandatory under 31-49g(b)(3). CTPL-003-CTRB(c) makes an employer that under-deducts liable for the shortfall and bars recouping it from future wages without CT DOL permission. So an employer that skips withholding ends up bearing the cost, but as a compliance failure, not a lawful election. CTRB(a)(4) adds that money collected from employees is held in trust for remittance.

Is the employee ever liable? Yes, in two places:
- 31-49g(b)(4) allows collection from the employee.
- CTRB(i) makes an employee subject to the same penalties when contributions go unpaid for reasons in the employee's control, such as tipped income they did not disclose.

The secondary sources conflict, and I relied on neither. The Hartford says employers are "prohibited" from contributing on employees' behalf in the state program. Payroll vendors say employers may cover it voluntarily.

The real optional pass-through is the approved private plan under 31-49o(c). There, employees owe nothing to the state fund, and the employer "may withhold or divert up to" the state-rate share. Excluded public employers (unless their workers bargain in), work outside Connecticut, and non-enrolled self-employed people owe $0. The prompt does not rule these out, but none of them changes the default program's classification.

2026 rate and cap:
- 0.5%: board vote Sept. 11, 2025, under the policy requiring any change to be announced by Nov. 1.
- $184,500: Federal Register, Nov. 3, 2025.
- Both predate 2026-07-03.

Statute: UIC 984(a)(1) says "Each worker shall pay worker contributions", and s. 2901 repeats this. UIC 986(a)(1) says each employer "shall" withhold the contribution in trust from wages when they are paid. Under 986(a)(2), an employer that agrees to pay the contribution without deducting it must still hold the amount in trust and send it in (986(b)). The employer has no SDI rate of its own under the State Plan (986(b) contrasts the worker contributions with the employer's "own contributions for the Unemployment Fund").

Administration lens:
- Regulation: 22 CCR 986-1 (read on LII) says employee contributions "shall be deducted by the employer".
- EDD guidance: the DE 44, the Employer Requirements page and the Contribution Rates page describe SDI as mandatory employee payroll deductions. "Employers must: Withhold mandatory payroll deductions for DI and PFL." The DE 44 says "Who Pays? Employee".
- Paying the employee share: the employer may pay it instead of deducting it (DE 231Q; s. 986(a)(2)). This mirrors the FICA option. The amount the employer pays becomes extra SDI-subject wages, grossed up as W = S/(1-R) with R = .0130 for 2026. So the contribution is still owed on the worker's wages; only who funds it changes. That is the reverse of an optional pass-through, where the premium is the employer's liability and deducting is discretionary.
- Liability if not deducted: I found no rule that makes the employee liable to the state. Collection runs against the employer: UIC 1126 assesses "employer and worker contributions payable by the employing unit", s. 1112 imposes a 15% penalty on an employer that fails to pay contributions "required of ... his or her workers", s. 1113 adds interest, and s. 1735 makes responsible officers personally liable. This makes the withholding duty enforceable. It does not make it optional.

The only genuinely optional pass-through is an approved Voluntary Plan. Under one, neither the employee nor the employer owes the State Plan contribution (s. 3252(a)). The employer "may, but need not" bear the cost and may deduct up to the State Plan amount (s. 3260; DE 2040). A VP needs majority employee consent and EDD approval (s. 3254), and the benchmark prompt gives no facts suggesting one. Other narrow carve-outs are the religious exemption (s. 2902) and coverage exclusions (public entities except as listed in s. 2606, some domestic workers, and others). None of them is triggered by the household facts.

Rate and cap: 1.3% for 2026 on all wages with no cap. The no-cap rule comes from s. 985(b), enacted by SB 951 (approved 2022-09-30) as amended by SB 143 (effective 2023-09-13). The rate was published on EDD's site by 2025-11-07/10 and in the DE 201 (created 2025-12-03), DE 3395 (2025-12-17), the VP letter (2025-12-31), the DI forecast (2026-01-07) and DE 44 (2026-04-17), all before 2026-07-03.

research.summary:
This is a mandatory employee contribution collected by mandatory employer withholding, not an optional employer pass-through.

- **Who owes it:** UC Law s. 301.4(a) (43 P.S. s. 781.4) says each employe "shall pay" contributions on all wages for covered employment, "without regard to" the $10,000 s. 4(x)(1) limit.
- **How it is collected:** s. 301.4(b) says each employer "shall withhold, in trust" the contributions and send them to the Department. Section 301.4(c) penalizes failing to withhold.
- **Employer election:** I found no provision letting an employer pay the employee contribution instead of withholding it, in the statute, in the 34 Pa. Code ch. 63 table of contents, or on the DLI pages. DLI says all employers, reimbursable ones included, must withhold.
- **2026 rate:** 0.07% of gross wages with no cap. Sources are DLI's UC-749 REV 09-25 rate chart (created September 2025; it records the July 1, 2025 trigger at 119%) and a PA Office of the Budget memo of January 13, 2026. Both predate 2026-07-03.
- **Engine:** pa_employee_unemployment_compensation_contribution = 0.0007 x employment_income, with no cap.
- **Engine vs. law:** scenario_028 is $60,000 x 0.0007 = $42.00, and scenario_123 is $145,000 x 0.0007 = $101.50. Both match the law exactly, and I confirmed both by running the engine. Because the rate is flat and uncapped, the result does not depend on how wages are split.
- **Main caveat:** the engine applies the rate to all wages of PA residents. The law applies to covered employment localized in PA and excludes listed services such as clergy, student workers and family employment.

I could not refute the classification. I read the official PA General Assembly text of UC Law Article III (Chapter 3) in full for ss. 301, 301.4, 301.7 and 301.8, and the Article I s. 4 definitions (Chapter 1) myself.

What the statute says:

- **How it is collected.** s. 301.4(b) says each employer 'shall be responsible for withholding and shall withhold, in trust' those contributions from wages when the wages are paid.
- **Penalty.** s. 301.4(c) applies penalties to an employer or officer who 'fails to withhold'.
- **Definitions.** s. 4(g) says 'Contributions' also means payments 'required to be paid ... by employes'.

- I searched Chapter 3 for 'deduct', 'withh', 'in lieu', 'on behalf of', 'without deduction', 'may pay' and 'employe shall'. No 'may deduct' language and no employer-election clause turned up.

- The 2026 rate of 0.07% follows from s. 301.8(b)(1): the trigger was 119%, below 250%, so the redetermined rates apply. The figure itself is published in UC-749 REV 09-25 (September 2025) and the BCPO memo (January 13, 2026), both before the 2026-07-03 cutoff.

Administration lens. On 'may' versus 'must', every primary source I read uses mandatory language and none uses 'may'. The statute (s. 301.4(b), official palegis.us text) says the employer 'shall be responsible for withholding and shall withhold, in trust'. DLI's employee-withholding page says 'all employers are required to withhold … regardless of whether an employer is contributory or reimbursable'. The reimbursable-employers page says the same, 'regardless of the method used to pay UC liability'. The yearly highlights say the contribution 'applies to all employees … and is not subject to appeal'. UCP-36 says both employer types 'are required to withhold'.

The liability sits on the employee: s. 301.4(a) says 'each employe shall pay contributions'. Section 4(g) defines 'Contributions' to include 'money payments required to be paid … by employes'. This is a separate employee tax, not a share of an employer premium. DLI says it is not credited to the employer's reserve account, and it is not a FUTA-certified contribution.

On whether an employer can choose to pay it, I found no provision allowing that. I checked s. 301.4, the full text of 34 Pa. Code chs. 61, 63 and 65, and the DLI employer pages. The only 'employer pays without deduction' language is s. 4(x)(3), and it concerns the federal FICA employee tax. I found no express prohibition either. The mandatory 'shall withhold' plus the s. 301.4(c) penalty for failing to withhold leave no lawful opt-out.

On employee liability if nothing is withheld, the statute is silent. Enforcement through s. 301.4(c), and from there ss. 301(a)(2), 308-309, runs against the employer and its officers and agents (interest, liens, civil collection, injunction). DLI warns of fines, prosecution and personal liability for the employer and its officers. I found no rule making the employee pay an unwithheld amount and no employer recovery right. The employee's s. 301.4(a) duty stands regardless. This gap does not turn the program into an optional pass-through, because the employer has no discretion.

The 2026 rate, the absence of a cap and the employer-only $10,000 base are confirmed by pre-cutoff primary sources. Section 301.8's five-year redetermination explains why 0.07% runs from 2023 through 2027.

research.premium_liability: The worker. Under N.J.S.A. 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)(i), each worker of a covered employer "shall ... make contributions" to the State disability benefits fund (TDI). Under (G)(ii), each worker "shall contribute" to the Family Temporary Disability Leave Account (FLI). Under 43:21-7(d)(1)(E), the employer must withhold those contributions in trust from wages and send them to the controller. The employer owes its own separate TDI contribution under 43:21-7(e)(1), which "shall not be deducted" from wages. FLI has no employer contribution at all. The liability moves to the employer only as a sanction: if it fails to deduct by the next payroll, "he alone shall thereafter be liable", and the amount is treated as an employer contribution for collection. Under an approved private plan, the employer funds the benefits. The employer may then charge employees up to the State-plan worker rate, or charge them nothing.

research.can_employer_elect_to_pay_employee_share: Under the State plan: no. The statute grants no election. 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)(i)-(ii) imposes the contribution on each worker, and 43:21-7(d)(1)(E) says the employer "shall ... withhold in trust" the workers' contributions, "notwithstanding any provision of law ... to the contrary". In practice an employer can end up bearing the worker share: if it fails to deduct by the next succeeding payroll, "he alone shall thereafter be liable" and cannot recover the amount. The statute frames that as the consequence of a failure, not as an authorized option. NJDOL's employer packet (2012, revised 2019) does describe deduction as a "right". Under an approved private plan (TDI and/or FLI): yes. The employer funds the plan and "may" collect employee contributions by payroll deduction (43:21-33), capped at the State-plan worker rate (43:21-32(d)). It may therefore charge less or nothing (a non-contributory plan). Sources: N.J.S.A. 43:21-7(d)(1)(E), (G); 43:21-32(d); 43:21-33.

caveats: Approved private plans (43:21-32, -33): an employer may replace the State plan for TDI, FLI or both. Its workers then pay no State-fund contribution for that program ((G)(i), (G)(ii)). Instead, the employer may charge them up to the State-plan worker rate, or nothing for a non-contributory plan. For those workers the employee share is optional for the employer, which is the one pass-through-like feature. The engine applies State-plan rates regardless.

Collective bargaining: if employees under a collective bargaining agreement are to contribute to a private plan, a majority must agree by written election, unless the agreement expressly waives that right (43:21-33). Employees not covered by an agreement need no consent.

Governmental employers: the State of New Jersey, Rutgers and NJIT are TDI covered employers. Other political subdivisions and instrumentalities are not covered for TDI unless they elect coverage (43:21-27(a)(1)-(2)), so their workers pay no TDI contribution. FLI covers governmental employers that are UI employers even without an election (43:21-27(a)(1); (G)(ii)).
Religious exemption (43:21-31): a person who relies on spiritual healing and files a waiver is exempt from the TDB Law, including any obligation to make contributions.

Employer status: worker contributions accrue only after the employer becomes an 'employer' subject to the UC law (43:21-19(h)). I did not verify the size or wage threshold for that status this session.

Failure to deduct: if the employer misses the current and next payroll, it alone is liable for the worker contributions (43:21-7(d)(1)(E)). A worker whose employer never deducted would actually pay $0.

Multiple employers: the $171,100 base applies per employer for withholding. A worker can claim a refund of anything above the annual maximum (43:21-7(d)(3)). The engine caps total employment_income per person, which matches the net after that refund.

research.summary:
New Jersey TDI and FLI worker contributions are mandatory and owed by the employee, and the employer must withhold them; they are not an optional employer pass-through.
- N.J.S.A. 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)(i) says each worker "shall ... make contributions" to the State disability benefits fund (TDI). (G)(ii) says each worker "shall contribute" to the Family Temporary Disability Leave Account (FLI).
- 43:21-7(d)(1)(E) requires each employer, "notwithstanding any provision of law ... to the contrary", to "withhold in trust" those contributions from wages. If it fails to deduct by the next payroll, the employer alone becomes liable.
- The employer's own TDI contribution (0.10% to 0.75% on $44,800) is separate and may not be deducted from wages. FLI is 100% worker-funded.
- The one exception that makes the employee share optional is an approved private plan (43:21-32, -33). There the employer "may" collect employee contributions, capped at the State-plan worker rate, or charge nothing.
- Other narrower carve-outs: non-electing local governmental employers (TDI only), the religious exemption, and collective-bargaining election rules for contributory private plans.

2026 figures:
- Worker TDI is 0.19% and FLI is 0.23% of the first $171,100, for maximums of $325.09 and $393.53.
- The wage base was proposed in 57 N.J.R. 1913(a) on 2025-09-02 and announced by NJDOL on 2025-12-29.
- The rates appear on undated NJDOL pages and were reported by 2025-11-04. All of this predates 2026-07-03.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute the research. The primary sources I read myself support 'mandatory_employee_withholding' for the State-plan TDI and FLI worker contributions the engine counts.

Statute lens: I read all of 43:21-7(d)(1)(A)-(G), (d)(3)-(6), (e)(1)-(2) and (b)(4) in NJDOL's Dec 2024 compilation, plus 43:21-27(a)-(b), -31, -32, -33 and -34 in the TDB Law compilation. The mandatory language runs both ways:
- Worker liability: (G)(i) says each worker 'shall ... make contributions'; (G)(ii) says each worker 'shall contribute'. (F) says 'contributions' in the chapter include workers' contributions.
- Employer duty: (E) says each employer 'shall, notwithstanding any provision of law ... to the contrary, withhold in trust' the workers' contributions. It must also show the deduction on payroll records and transmit it.
- Other sections confirm it. 43:21-14.4 (same compilation) refers to 'any contribution which the employer is required to collect from his employees' for the State disability benefits fund and the FLI account. 43:21-33 calls the State-plan withholding 'that deduction required by Revised Statutes, section 43:21-7(d)(1)'. 43:21-32 says workers excluded from a private plan are 'subject to the employee contribution required by law'.

The only 'may deduct' language in the chapter is in 43:21-33, and it applies only to an approved private plan. There the employer may collect contributions, capped at the State-plan worker rate by 43:21-32(d).

The two strongest refutation levers do not hold:
- Failure to deduct: if the employer misses the current and next payroll, it 'alone shall thereafter be liable'. That is a sanction attached to a duty, not an election. The amount is then 'treated as employer's contributions' only for collection under 43:21-14.
- The 'right to deduct' wording in NJDOL's 2012 employer packet (revised 2019): agency guidance phrasing cannot override the statute's 'shall withhold'. The same paragraph repeats the failure-to-deduct liability, and NJDOL's current worker pages describe the contribution as a salary deduction 'your employer takes'.

The employer's own TDI contribution under (e)(1) is separate and 'shall not be deducted' from wages. FLI has no employer contribution: the statute imposes (G)(ii) on workers only, and NJDOL confirms '100% by worker payroll deductions'.

Exceptions do not change the default for household-only prompts. These are approved private plans, non-electing local governmental employers (TDI only; FLI still applies under the second 'covered employer' definition in 43:21-27(a)(1)), the 43:21-31 religious waiver, and the collective bargaining election for contributory private plans. The research flagged each as a caveat accurately.

Both match 0.19% and 0.23% of $26,800.

Remaining weaknesses are documentary, not substantive:
- There is no dated official source for the 2026 worker rates. The statutory posting deadline and a Nov 2025 secondary article support pre-cutoff publication.
- The wage-base rule is cited as a proposal, and I did not verify its adoption.
- The NJ Legislature's site was unreachable, so I could not rule out post-compilation amendments.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute the classification from the administration side and could not.

STATUTE (official NJDOL compilations, downloaded and text-extracted this session)
- 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)(i): each worker of a covered employer 'shall ... make contributions' for TDI.
- 43:21-7(d)(1)(G)(ii): each worker 'shall contribute' for FLI. FLI coverage includes governmental UI employers.
- 43:21-7(d)(1)(E): each employer 'shall, notwithstanding any provision of law ... to the contrary, withhold in trust' those contributions.
- 43:21-7(e)(1): the employer's own TDI contribution 'shall not be deducted' from wages.

ADMINISTRATIVE RULES
- N.J.A.C. 12:16-9.1(a) (read via LII): 'Every employer shall withhold workers' contributions from their wages at each time of payment of such wages.' 12:16-9.3 requires the remittance to include contributions 'payable by the employer on behalf of its workers'.
- N.J.A.C. 12:18-2.1(b)-(c) and 2.21(a) (NJDOL 2011 compilation): the employer 'shall be liable for the deduction' of workers' contributions whenever workers are on the State plan.

AGENCY GUIDANCE FOR 2026
- The current NJDOL employer page says employers 'must participate ... and deduct payroll taxes'. The only alternative it offers is a private plan.
- The worker TDI and FLI pages say a covered employer is 'required to set up payroll contributions for you'.
- The one 'may'-style phrasing is in the 2012 (rev. 2019) Employer Informational Packet: employers 'have the right to deduct'. In context that sentence is about timing: deduct in the current or next payroll or lose the ability. It does not grant an option to absorb the share.

CAN THE EMPLOYER CHOOSE TO PAY THE EMPLOYEE SHARE?
- Under the State plan, no statute, rule or page grants that election.
- An employer that fails to deduct by the next payroll becomes 'alone' liable, and the amount is collected as an employer contribution. That is a de facto consequence of non-compliance with a 'shall withhold' duty, not an authorized pass-through.

IS THE EMPLOYEE LIABLE IF THE AMOUNT IS NOT DEDUCTED?
- Generally no. The statute puts sole liability on the employer.
- The narrow exception is 43:21-7(d)(4). When wages are paid by a different employing unit, the employer is liable 'in the first instance'. It may then recover from that unit or, absent one, from the individual in a civil action within three months.
- So in practice an employee whose employer never withheld pays $0. This matches the researcher's caveat and does not change the classification under the task's definition ('the employer must withhold it').

WHERE THE SHARE IS GENUINELY OPTIONAL
Only under an approved private plan. Under 43:21-33 the employer 'may' collect contributions, capped at the State-plan rate by 43:21-32(d). It may therefore charge less or nothing. The researcher already identified this.

2026 RATES, WAGE BASE AND DATES
- Rates 0.19% (TDI) and 0.23% (FLI) and the $171,100 wage base are confirmed on current NJDOL pages and in 57 N.J.R. 1913(a) (2025-09-02).
- The NJDOL press release of 2025-12-29 gives a 2024 AWW of $1,598.66; 107 x $1,598.66 = $171,056.62, which rounds up to $171,100.
- Wayback captures show the official rate-info page listing the 2026 worker rates by 2025-11-05. All of this predates 2026-07-03.

ENGINE CHECK
- I read the NJ variables and parameters this session. Each contribution is the rate times min(max(0, employment_income), $171,100). The NJ files carry no 'maximum permitted employee share' assumption.
- For scenario_008 the engine gives $50.92 TDI and $61.64 FLI, which equals the law's State-plan required amounts exactly.

RESIDUAL GAPS (none undercut the classification)
- I could not reach the NJ Legislature site to rule out post-2024 amendments to 43:21-7.
- The 12:16 rule text came from LII, not the official code.
- Current 2026 agency pages remain consistent with mandatory withholding.

programs.premium_liability: ESD assesses a premium on each individual's wages (RCW 50A.10.030(1)).
